She measures the flour carefully, presses the butter between her fingertips, and tastes the dough the way Grandma does, from the very tip of a spoon. Grandma corrects the angle of her wrist, taps the side of the bowl twice for luck, and tells her about the time her own grandmother let her bake bread in a tin too big for the oven. The first batch spreads into flat, brown puddles. The second batch is better. By the third, Asha can tell by the smell when they are done. That evening the whole family eats warm biscuits, and Grandma taps the notebook. 'Now it is your recipe too,' she says. 'But do not write down the weather. Some things you just know.' Asha thinks about that as she licks melted butter off her thumb, and writes on the last page: 'Rain means extra ginger.'

passages.title: The Night Train
passages.text: The train leaves the station at nine o'clock at night, and Leo has never travelled so late. He presses his forehead to the window as the platform slides away and the town turns into strings of orange lights. Dad has packed a bag of snacks and two pairs of headphones, but Leo finds he does not need music. The map on the table shows the whole journey, but the window shows it better. In the dark window, the train's reflection rides along on top of the real fields, and for a while it looks like two trains racing, one made of light. At the first stop, a woman with a violin case gets on and sits opposite. She winks at Leo and lets him guess what is inside the case. 'A tennis racket,' he says. 'A dragon,' he says. She laughs and shows him the violin. When the ticket inspector comes, she plays a quiet tune to make the punch in his ticket feel like a drumroll. Leo falls asleep somewhere after midnight and wakes as the train slows into Grandma's station, where she is waiting on the platform with a thermos and two cups. 'Did you see anything good?' she asks. 'Everything,' says Leo, and it almost feels true.

passages.title: The Winning Goal
passages.text: Chloe's team has not scored a single goal all season, and today is the last match. The parents on the touchline have stopped shouting 'shoot' and started shouting 'well done' for every pass, which is what the coach asked them to do. Chloe plays in goal, and she has spent most of the season watching the ball at the other end of the pitch. Today is different. In the second half, the wind picks up behind her team. The other side kicks the ball high, and the wind brings it back down like a dropped parcel, right at Chloe's feet. Everyone shouts for her to kick it long. Instead she rolls it out to Priya, the smallest player on the pitch, who has been waiting all season for the ball to come to her. Priya runs. The wind pushes at her back. Chloe has never seen anyone run that fast, and from the far end it looks like Priya is outrunning the wind itself. The shot bounces off the post and in. The final whistle goes a minute later, and the score is one-nil to Chloe's team. The parents' 'well done' turns into the loudest cheering of the year. Chloe's glove smells of grass for days, and every time she catches it, she smiles.

passages.title: How Bees Make Honey
passages.text: Honey begins with flowers. A bee visits a flower to drink its nectar, a sweet liquid hidden deep inside the bloom. The bee stores the nectar in a special stomach and carries it back to the hive. There, hive bees pass the nectar to one another and add special substances that start to change it. Then they put the nectar into the small wax cells of the honeycomb and fan it with their wings. The fanning dries the nectar out until it becomes thick, golden honey. A honeycomb cell is capped with a wax lid, sealing the honey in like a jar. Inside, the hive stays warm all winter, which keeps the colony safe and busy. A single bee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life, so every jar in the shop is the work of thousands of bees. Bees make honey to feed the colony through the winter, when there are no flowers to visit. Beekeepers collect only some of the honey, leaving the rest for the bees. That is why a spoonful of honey on your toast is such a remarkable thing: it is flower nectar, carried home drop by drop, and turned into treasure by wings.

passages.title: The Water Cycle
passages.text: The water in your glass has been on Earth for billions of years, travelling in a great loop called the water cycle. It starts when the Sun warms water in seas, lakes, and puddles. Some of that water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour, rising into the sky like a slow, silent elevator. High up, where the air is cold, the vapour cools and gathers into millions of tiny droplets, forming clouds. When the droplets bump into each other and grow too heavy to float, they fall as rain, hail, or snow. The water soaks into soil, flows into streams and rivers, and makes its way back to the sea, where the whole journey begins again. Some of the rain that falls today may have fallen on dinosaurs, watered ancient farms, or been sipped by a polar bear. Even the puddle outside your school and the ice in your drink are travellers on the same long road. Scientists say there is no new water being made on Earth, which means every drop is recycled. So the water you drink really has been around the world, and now it is passing through you on its next trip around the loop. So when you pour a glass, try to imagine its journey so far, and where it might go next.

passages.title: Roman Roads
passages.text: About two thousand years ago, Roman soldiers and engineers built a huge network of roads across their empire so that armies could march quickly and messages could travel fast. Roman roads were built to last. First, workers dug a trench and filled it with big stones for a strong base. Then came layers of smaller stones, pebbles, and sand, all packed down firmly. The top was paved with flat stones, often sloping slightly so rain would run off into ditches at the sides. Many Roman roads were so straight that some are still used as roads today, and you can walk on original Roman paving in places like Britain, Italy, and Spain. Some modern roads still follow the old Roman routes, because the straightest way across a valley is often still the straightest way. The Romans even used stones called milestones that marked the distance to the nearest town, so travellers always knew how far they had to go. When Roman rule ended, the roads remained, and later travellers, farmers, and builders used the same routes for centuries. Ruts worn by Roman cart wheels can still be seen in places, deep grooves pressed into the stone. Next time you are on a long, straight road, remember: it might be following a path first stamped out by Roman boots.

passages.title: Living in Space
passages.text: Living on the International Space Station means floating. Because the station orbits Earth in a constant state of free fall, everything inside floats, from water drops to sleeping astronauts. Astronauts must strap themselves into sleeping bags attached to the walls, or they would drift away. There is no up or down, so the walls, floor, and ceiling can all be used, and some astronauts sleep on the ceiling just for fun. First-time visitors often bump their heads for days until their brains learn the new rules. Water is precious in space. Every drop, including the moisture astronauts breathe out, is cleaned and reused. A famous saying on the station is that yesterday's coffee becomes tomorrow's coffee. Meals come in packets, and salt and pepper are kept as liquid, because floating grains would get into the equipment. Astronauts exercise for about two hours every day on special machines, because without gravity their muscles and bones grow weaker. Even with all the hard work, astronauts say the best part is looking out of the window. From the station, Earth has no borders, no cities you can name, and no sound at all. It just glows, wrapped in its thin blue line of air, and every ninety minutes there is a brand new sunrise.

passages.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Cat
passages.text:
Old Marlow keeps the light on Seal Rock, and his cat, Biscuit, keeps Marlow. That is what Marlow tells the supply boat, and Biscuit does not argue. Every evening, when the lamp begins its slow turn, Biscuit climbs the one hundred and three spiral stairs to the lamp room, sits on the brass ledge, and watches the sea through the glass. Marlow polishes the great lens and pretends he is not talking to her. 'Fishermen out there,' he says, 'would trade their boots for your eyes.' Biscuit blinks. Her eyes are the colour of harbour water.

One evening in November, the weather turns wild before the forecast has finished saying it might. Waves shoulder the rocks, and the wind throws salt against the tower like handfuls of gravel. Marlow lights the lamp early and makes his last round of the railings. That is when he misses a step and comes down hard on his wrist. He hears the small click of something not right, and the wrist swells like rising dough. The radio hisses. The supply boat will not come until morning, and the lamp must be wound every four hours, or it stops.

Biscuit watches him sit down on the stair with his face the colour of porridge. Then she does something she has never done. She climbs down all one hundred and three stairs, pushes through the draught door, and wails at the dark. Out in the storm, a fishing boat is beating its way home. The crew see two lights: the great lamp, and a small, fierce shape at the tower door, glowing yellow in the beam as it cries. They radio the coastguard, and the lifeboat crew know Biscuit's voice of old.

Marlow winds the lamp that night with one hand and Biscuit's considerable help. In the morning, his wrist is set at the clinic on the mainland, and he is back before the next storm. On the supply boat's manifest, in the box marked 'reason for visit', the skipper writes: 'cat.'

From then on, Marlow winds the lamp early, keeps his boots by the door, and never once says cats are no use at sea. Biscuit, for her part, keeps the ledge warm, and the lighthouse keeps its two keepers: one with a torch, one with a tail.

passages.title: The Time Capsule
passages.text:
Under the floorboards of Number 9, behind a pile of rubble that smells of forgotten summers, Tayo finds a biscuit tin. Inside, wrapped in a scarf that has gone the colour of weak tea, are objects arranged like a small museum: a marble, a tram ticket, a photograph of a street party with flags strung across the road, and a letter in careful handwriting that begins, 'Whoever finds this, hello from 1953.'

The letter is from a boy called Albert, who writes that he has included his best marble because the future probably has better ones, and he wants the finder to know what mattered to him. Tayo reads it three times on the stairs. Then he does what any sensible person would do. He takes the tin to school, where his class is exactly halfway through a project about how people lived in the past, and his teacher, Miss Adeyemi, goes very quiet, which for Miss Adeyemi is the loudest possible reaction.

The class visits the local history room at the library, where a white-haired volunteer reads Albert's letter through spectacles that slip down her nose. 'Albert Matravers,' she says at last. 'He sat in the seat by the window. He lost that marble every single week.' She shows them the street in the photograph, and the children count the changes: the bakery has become a bank, the cinema has become flats, and Number 9's door is exactly the same red.

Miss Adeyemi has an idea, and the idea becomes a plan, and the plan becomes a hole in the school garden, lined with a plastic box. Every child adds one object and a letter. Tayo contributes a pen drive and a letter that begins, 'Whoever finds this, hello from now. We found Albert. Here is what mattered to him.'

Years are long when you are ten, but the box has a date on it that is safely far away, and that night Tayo thinks about Albert pressing his marble into the dark and trusting a stranger to be curious. Being curious, Tayo decides, is a kind of thank-you. He falls asleep wondering whose hands will unwrap his pen drive, and whether they will think it is marvellous or ridiculous, and hoping, fiercely, for both.

passages.title: The Marathon
passages.text:
On race morning, Dee stands at the start line with eight thousand other runners and tries to remember why this seemed like a good idea. The answer is pinned to her vest in the form of a paper number, and underneath the number is a photo of her grandad, who ran this marathon fifty years ago in boots that were too small, according to family legend, 'for the glory of it.'

Dee's trainers cost more than Grandad's first car, and she has trained for six months, and still the first mile is a surprise. It is crowded and slow and joyful. Children hold out oranges. A brass band plays something fast at the wrong moment. At mile eight, a man in a tomato costume passes her like she is standing still, and Dee laughs so much she nearly forgets to run.

The hard part comes later, as the hard part does. At mile twenty, Dee's legs begin to argue with the plan, and the crowd's noise turns to soup. She thinks about stopping. Then she sees her family at the side of the road, holding a sign that says 'GO GRANDAD'S BOOTS,' and something in her chest stands up straight. She picks a runner ahead with a bright yellow hat and makes a deal: reach the yellow hat, then find a new one.

The last mile bends toward the finish, and Dee hears her own name coming over the loudspeaker, badly pronounced and entirely wonderful. She crosses the line one hour and fifty-two minutes faster than Grandad's boots ever managed, though she notes the boots did it without energy drinks or a brass band. The medal goes straight into an envelope addressed to him, with a note: 'Same race. Same glory. Better shoes.'

That winter, the photo of Grandad crosses the finish line in Dee's frame, boots and all, hung at the exact height where neither of them has to look up or down to see it.

passages.title: The Lost Notebook
passages.text:
Mr Alvarez gives out the science notebooks on Monday, and by Friday afternoon, Mari's is missing. She has looked in her tray, her bag, the lost property box, and once, in a moment of madness, the boys' cloakroom. The notebook matters more than most. Inside it are six weeks of experiment notes, one pressed flower from a habitat survey, and the first draft of her project on how plants drink, which is due after the weekend.

Mari retraces her week like a detective. The last definite sighting, according to her lab partner Sam, is Thursday's fieldwork, when Mari knelt in the long grass by the pond and the notebook was under her knee. After that: nothing. On Saturday morning she goes back to the pond with her mum, telling herself she is only walking the dog, who has no idea he is part of a search party.

The pond is Friday-night still. Mari works along the bank, parting grass with her hands, while the dog patrols importantly. Near the willow, something blue peeks through the reeds. It is her notebook, damp at the corners but complete, held down by a flat grey stone as if someone meant to keep it from blowing away. Tucked inside the cover is a note in joined-up writing: 'Found this Thursday. Did not know whose it was. Left it where it fell. Good luck with the plants. From a fellow scientist.'

Mari takes the notebook home and dries the pages one by one. She never finds out who the fellow scientist is, though she narrows it to three suspects: the jogger with the red hat, the man who feeds the ducks, or the keeper who locks the gates. Her project gets a gold star and a comment: 'Excellent observations. Also, excellent pressing.'

On the last page of her notebook, Mari copies out the stranger's note, and underneath writes: 'Kindness is a method. Results may vary.' It becomes the motto of every project she does for the rest of the year, and several that she does not.

passages.title: The Orchestra
passages.text:
An orchestra is a team of musicians who play together under a leader called the conductor. A full symphony orchestra can have around one hundred players, and every one of them has a seat in a plan, laid out so the sound reaches the audience in balance. The strings sit at the front: dozens of violins, violas, cellos, and deep, rumbling double basses. Behind them come the woodwind, instruments like flutes, clarinets, and oboes, whose players blow across or through reeds to make their sound. The brass section, with trumpets, trombones, and tubas, can play so loudly that composers sometimes give them the tune in the grandest moments. At the very back sit the percussionists, who play the drums, cymbals, and timpani, and beside them, the pianist or harpist if the music needs them.

Every section speaks a slightly different language. Strings can swoop and whisper, woodwind can chirp and sigh, brass can blaze, and percussion can mark time like a heartbeat or explode like thunder. The conductor's job is to listen to all of this at once and shape it. With a wave of the baton, the conductor sets the speed, shows the loud and soft, and reminds dozens of musicians to come in at exactly the right moment. Players watch the conductor constantly, but they also listen to each other, because a great orchestra is really one instrument with a hundred voices.

You do not have to be grown up to play in one. Youth orchestras welcome young players every year, and the youngest might start with just three notes and a rattle. The first time all the sections play together, children say, the feeling is like being lifted off the chair. Music teachers say it is also very good for you: reading music, counting, watching, listening, and breathing all at once. Perhaps that is the secret of the orchestra. It is not just a hundred people playing instruments. It is a hundred people learning to be one.

passages.title: Wild Weather
passages.text:
Weather is the conversation between the Sun, the air, and the water on Earth, and sometimes that conversation gets loud. A thunderstorm begins when warm, moist air rises quickly and meets colder air high above. Inside the cloud, water droplets and ice bump into each other and swap tiny electric charges, until the cloud is like a battery storing up energy. When the difference grows too great, it releases as a bolt of lightning that heats the air around it so fast that the air cracks apart, making thunder. Because light travels faster than sound, we see the flash before we hear the bang, and counting the seconds between them tells you roughly how far away the storm is. Every three seconds between flash and bang means the storm is about a kilometre away.

Snow is the quieter member of the family. It forms when water vapour freezes high in the sky into ice crystals that stick together as they fall. No two snowflakes are exactly alike, scientists tell us, and each flake is a pattern made of frozen water with air trapped inside, which is why fresh snow squeaks underfoot. A single snowflake is feather-light, yet a whole storm of them can close roads, snap branches, and build drifts taller than a door.

The strangest weather of all may be the dust devil, a spinning column of air that skitters across dry ground on hot days, picking up dust and leaves. Unlike a tornado, it forms on clear days and is usually small and short-lived, though it can still tip a wheelie bin or scatter a picnic. Whether storm, snow, or spinning dust, all of it is the same Earthly engine at work: the Sun pouring energy down, and the air and water passing that energy along. Wild weather is not wild at all, really. It is physics, wearing a very dramatic coat.

passages.title: The Solar System
passages.text:
Everything you have ever touched, everyone you have ever met, and every mountain and ocean on Earth is part of one family called the solar system. At the centre sits the Sun, an ordinary middle-aged star that holds the whole system together with its gravity. It is so massive that more than a million Earths could fit inside it, and it makes up more than 99 percent of all the mass in the solar system.

Travelling outward from the Sun, eight planets ride their looping orbits. The four inner planets are rocky worlds like Earth: Mercury, the speedy one, races around the Sun in just 88 days; Venus hides under thick clouds; Earth is the only world known to have oceans and life; and Mars, the red one, hosts the tallest volcano in the system, a mountain called Olympus Mons. Beyond Mars stretches the asteroid belt, a ring of rocky leftovers, some as small as pebbles and one, Ceres, big enough to be called a dwarf planet.

The outer four planets are giants. Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for centuries. Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice, some as small as grains of sand. Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, and Neptune, the farthest planet, takes 165 Earth years to complete a single trip. Beyond them lie icy comets and more dwarf planets, including Pluto, in a dark, cold region called the Kuiper Belt.

The solar system is big in a way that is hard to imagine. If the Sun were the size of a football on a playing field, Earth would be a peppercorn about twenty-five metres away, and Neptune would be a blueberry near the edge of the field, nearly eight hundred paces from the ball. Yet this whole enormous neighbourhood is just one tiny corner of the Milky Way, which itself is one galaxy among billions. Small, it turns out, is a matter of where you stand.

passages.title: From Wheat to Bread
passages.text:
Long before your loaf reaches the kitchen, it begins in a field of wheat, standing taller than your knee and rippling like a golden sea in the wind. Wheat is a grass that farmers have grown for more than ten thousand years, and it is one of the most important crops in the world. In early summer the crop turns from green to gold, and when the grains are hard and dry, a combine harvester moves through the field, cutting the stalks and separating the grain from the straw in one enormous pass. The straw is left behind in neat rows, and many farmers gather it up to use as bedding for animals or to mix back into the soil.

The grain then travels to a mill, where rollers crush it in stages until it becomes flour. White flour is sieved to remove the brown outer layers, while wholemeal flour keeps everything the grain contains. Meanwhile, at the bakery, flour meets water, salt, and yeast. The dough is kneaded, rested so the yeast can fill it with bubbles, shaped into tins or rolls, and baked in an oven hot enough to turn the outside golden and crisp. Steam inside the loaf makes the inside soft, and the smell that drifts from a bakery vent is a mixture of toasted grain, warm yeast, and sugar that the heat has browned.

Bread is eaten in some form all over the planet, from flatbreads cooked on hot stones to tall loaves baked in tins, and for thousands of years it has been called the staff of life, meaning something people cannot do without. So the next time you hold a slice, follow its journey backwards: from plate, to bakery, to mill, to harvester, to a green shoot in a winter field. Simple food is rarely simple. It is a story, and you are holding the last page.
